Languish

LANG-gwish -- from Old French languir, from Latin languere ('to be faint, weak'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To languish is to remain in an unpleasant or neglected state for a long time, gradually growing weaker.

Overshadowed by flashier startups, the once-promising app languished for years with barely any new users.

Worked Example

After the theater lost its funding, the beautiful old building languished for a decade, its paint peeling and its seats gathering dust.

That slow, neglected decline over a long stretch of time -- not a sudden collapse -- is exactly what it means to languish.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

decay: Decay is physical rotting: wood, teeth, and old fruit decay as their material breaks down. Languish is about neglect rather than rot -- a career, a building, or a project languishes when it sits ignored and slowly weakens. Decayed things are being destroyed; languishing things could still be revived.

stagnate: To stagnate is to stop moving or developing, the way still water goes stale. Languish adds suffering and decline: whatever languishes is not merely stuck but wasting away in an unpleasant, neglected state. An economy can stagnate at a comfortable level, yet nothing comfortable ever languishes.

fade: To fade is to lose color, strength, or attention little by little, and it carries no sense of neglect or misery -- applause fades, tans fade, a hit song fades from the radio. To languish is grimmer: it means being stuck somewhere unpleasant, ignored, and growing weaker the whole time.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

prosper: to succeed and do well

rebound: to recover strength or popularity after a decline

Build the Word

The pieces

root — langu-

root — langu-: to be faint, weak (Latin (languere))

suffix — -ish

suffix — -ish: verb ending (as in finish, vanish) (French)

Put it together

Put it together: Languish comes from Latin languere, 'to be faint or weak,' with the French verb ending -ish, as in finish and vanish -- to languish is literally to grow weak and stay that way, worn down by neglect rather than any single sudden blow.

Use the root in a new word: languor

Use the root in a new word: languor: A heavy languor settled over the household in the sticky heat of August.
